sections.h2: Why trim deserves its own attention
body: Walls are seen from across the room. Trim is seen up close: you touch door casings, vacuums bump baseboards, and crown molding draws the eye along every ceiling line. Gaps, cracked caulk, gritty paint, and yellowed white make a house look tired even when the walls are fresh. Trim painting is slower, more detailed work, and it shows.

We paint trim on its own as a refresh, or as part of whole-room and whole-home interior painting. Trim-only projects are popular when the wall color still works but the woodwork is scuffed, or when owners want to brighten stained trim to a clean white.

Trim also sets the tone for the rest of the room: a crisp white casing makes a bold wall color look intentional, while a soft off-white suits warmer palettes. We can help you choose the right white during the walkthrough.

sections.h2: Prep is most of the job
body: Nail holes are filled and sanded flush so they disappear. Open miters, gaps where trim meets the wall, and splits are caulked and tooled to a clean line. Existing glossy paint is cleaned and scuff-sanded so the new coat bonds. Bare wood and patched areas are primed, and stained or knotty wood gets a stain-blocking primer so tannins and knots do not bleed through a white finish.

Between coats, trim is lightly sanded to knock down dust nibs that land while the paint is wet. That small step is the difference between a finish that feels smooth and one that feels like sandpaper. Floors and carpet are protected with tape and drop cloths so baseboard edges come out crisp.

Previously painted trim with many layers sometimes shows rounded, soft details or old drips. Where that build-up is bad, especially on window stools and door casings, crews scrape and sand back the worst areas so the profile reads crisply again. Damaged sections of baseboard or casing can be patched or replaced with matching profiles before painting, and that work is listed separately on the estimate.

Using wall paint on trim is a common shortcut, and it shows quickly. Wall paint stays relatively soft, sticks to itself where doors meet stops, and marks easily. We use a waterborne urethane enamel that cures to a hard, scrubbable film, levels out brush marks, and holds its white over time instead of yellowing like old oil enamel.

Semi-gloss and satin are the usual sheens: semi-gloss for maximum washability on baseboards and doors, satin for a softer look on paneling or crown. If your trim was previously painted in oil, a bonding primer is used so the waterborne enamel adheres. Our guide on choosing the right paint finish explains sheen in more detail.

Many homes built in the 1980s and 1990s have oak or pine trim in an orange-toned finish. Painting it white is one of the most dramatic updates you can make. The clear finish is cleaned and deglossed, then a bonding, stain-blocking primer goes on before two coats of enamel. Oak grain will still show some texture under paint, which most people like; if you want it smooth, grain filling can be added. The same thinking applies to oak cabinets, covered in our post on painting oak cabinets.
If you would rather keep the wood look and simply refresh it, see our wood staining and finishing service.

Exterior fascia, soffit, window trim, and corner boards take the most weather on a house and are usually where rot shows first. Those are handled with 100% acrylic exterior paint and rot repair through our exterior painting service, and shutters and doors through door and shutter painting.

Interior trim work is done room by room while you live in the home. A single room's trim is often a day; a whole house takes longer depending on how much detail there is. Your estimate lists exactly which trim is included, the products, sheen, and number of coats.

Afterward, trim cleans up with a damp cloth and mild soap. Give fresh enamel a few weeks to reach full hardness before scrubbing scuffs or closing doors firmly against new paint, and use the labelled touch-up we leave for any nicks that appear along the way.

faqs.q: What paint do you use on trim?
faqs.a: A waterborne urethane enamel, usually in semi-gloss or satin. It cures hard, cleans easily, and resists yellowing better than old oil enamels.

faqs.q: Can you paint only the trim?
faqs.a: Yes. Trim-only projects are common when the wall color still works. We protect the walls and cut clean lines along every edge.

faqs.q: Can stained oak trim be painted white?
faqs.a: Yes. It is cleaned, deglossed, and primed with a bonding, stain-blocking primer before two coats of enamel so tannins do not bleed through.

faqs.q: Why does my door stick to the frame after painting?
faqs.a: Usually because wall paint or a soft product was used, or the door was closed before the enamel cured. A proper trim enamel and cure time prevent it.
